The hangups. Why is the budget resolution so unpopular in the Senate Republican Conference?

There are those like Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) who won’t vote for anything that includes SAVE Act provisions.

“It doesn’t have the votes,” said Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), who backs the measure. “It is an exercise in futility if the votes aren’t there. Period, end of story. Do something productive with your life.”

Another big problem: Defense hawks say the House’s $67 billion for the Pentagon isn’t nearly enough amid the war in Iran and Trump’s massive $1.5 trillion FY2027 budget request.

Thune told us Monday he’d “prefer doubling” the defense number — and then suggested it may have to be bumped up to get 50 Senate Republicans on board.

“I do think that’s an issue,” Thune said in an interview. “Frankly, if we’re going to do this — and what it’s going to take to get this done — you kind of want to make it worthwhile. I think the president asked for $350 billion… We’re at $67 [billion].”

Thune also keeps warning about another vote-a-rama this close to the election. Vulnerable GOP senators don’t want to spend a night taking politically painful votes on Democratic amendments.

From Thune’s perspective, he needs to feel confident that Republicans can beat back all of the Democratic amendments. That’s going to be a big challenge.

But Sen. Mike Lee’s (R-Utah) is squeezing vulnerable Republicans further with his vow to force a vote on leaving for recess at the end of next week, when they’d rather be at home campaigning. It’s a name-and-shame move that would deepen GOP infighting without moving the SAVE whip count.

“Staying in doesn’t change what would happen on the SAVE Act,” Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), one of those vulnerable Republicans, said as she rattled off other bills she’d prioritize.

Attendance is a problem too. Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) is still out, costing Republicans a vote they need to get on the budget resolution before recess.

That is not an election.

O ex-chefe de gabinete do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), Marco Aurélio Santana Ribeiro, conhecido como Marcola, confirmou na segundaa (3) que recebeu valores da empresária e lobista Roberta Luchsinger, personagem investigada no caso das fraudes no INSS.

Em nota enviada à imprensa, Marcola afirmou que os recursos correspondiam a um empréstimo pessoal já quitado e negou qualquer irregularidade.

“Recebi com surpresa a matéria que trata um empréstimo pessoal contraído e já quitado como algo ilegal. Nunca tive nenhuma relação que caracterize qualquer ilegalidade no exercício de minha função”, declarou.

Marcola deixou o cargo no último dia 31 de julho, após atuar durante praticamente todo o terceiro mandato de Lula como chefe de gabinete da Presidência. Homem de confiança do presidente, era responsável pela coordenação da agenda presidencial e pelo atendimento direto das demandas encaminhadas ao chefe do Executivo.

O valor das transferências não foi informado pelo ex-assessor. O Poder360 apurou, com pessoas que acompanham o caso, que os pagamentos teriam girado em torno de R$ 80 mil, embora o montante e a frequência das operações não tenham sido oficialmente confirmados.
